title: Letter 1 — On the One Thing Needful
attribution_note: Translated for this edition from the Russian of St Tikhon of Zadonsk (public domain), from the collection he himself compiled under the title Letters Sent — 46 letters of counsel written from his retirement at Zadonsk, 1769–1780, to friends, pastors and people who wrote to him for advice. No English translation of this collection has been published; this is, as far as could be verified, the first. The Russian text the translation was made from is kept in the repository.

pairs.en: You asked me: what is our first task? I answer you. Consider it, and attend.

We were created for eternal life, and after the fall redeemed for it; by holy Baptism we were renewed, and by the Word of God called to eternal life; the Holy Scripture, given us from God, we have for the obtaining of eternal life; the Son of God, Jesus Christ, came into the world and lived in the world, suffered and died, so that we might obtain eternal life. You see, then, that the first and most necessary task of a Christian is his eternal salvation.

We need clothing, food, drink, a house and the rest; but eternal salvation is so necessary that without it everything is nothing. He has everything who has salvation, and he has nothing who has not salvation, though he held the whole world under his power. *“For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”* [Matthew 16:26]

Eternal salvation is the *one thing needful*, in Christ's own word; it is *the good part, which shall not be taken away* from us. [Luke 10:42] Everything we have in this world will be taken from us. Riches, honour, glory, comfort, friendship, wife, children, and this passing life itself will be taken away on the day of death; but the salvation of the soul, once found, is never taken away: it goes with the soul into the age to come, and to ages of ages is never parted from her.
This is your first Christian task. And this task is the very work of which Christ speaks to His heavenly Father: *“I have finished the work which Thou gavest Me to do.”* [John 17:4]

sections.heading: The first care of every calling

pairs.en: On the first task must be spent the first care, diligence, zeal, labour and struggle, that it may be brought to completion.

A soldier's first task is to be brave in battle, to stand against the enemy and defeat him; and so a good soldier's first care must be to be a good soldier. A servant's first task is to work for his master and please him; on this the good servant spends his first care. A pupil's first task is to study, and to learn from his teacher what he is being taught; on this his first care must be spent. A ruler's first task is to govern those in his charge and keep them in good order; his first care must be for that. A shepherd's first task is to pasture the flock entrusted to him; all his care must be that his flock stay whole. A judge's first task is to judge those who come to him for judgment, to search out the truth, to act justly and render to each his own; on this all his labour and care must be spent. And so with everything else.

Now for the Christian — since his first task is the task of salvation, as was said above — his first zeal, care, effort and struggle must be this: not to be deprived of the salvation that was found at so great a price, the Blood and death of Christ. Satan labours to take the Christian's eternal salvation from him; the Christian must labour not to lose it. The more the enemy strives for the Christian's ruin, the more the Christian must strive for his salvation.

The first task of the Christian, and the most necessary, is his salvation. Therefore always and everywhere his first care must be for it. His household, and all that belongs to this world, is his last task, and his care for it must come last; the very first is for the salvation of his soul — because everything else will leave him, but the soul's salvation, once obtained, will never leave. Let this thought, then, like a burning candle, go before him in all his works and undertakings, everywhere and always, and show him what he must do so as not to lose his salvation.

Is the Christian a judge? — let him so judge that he not fall under the eternal judgment of God. Is he a ruler? — let him so rule that he not be deprived of eternal salvation. Is he a pastor of Christ's flock? — let him so feed Christ's sheep that he destroy neither himself nor them. Is he a teacher? — let him so teach people that he save both himself and them. Is he a master? — let him so govern that he ruin neither himself nor his servants. Is he a father? — let him so deal with his children that he save them and himself. Is he a merchant? — let him so trade that he not destroy himself. Is he rich? — let him so use his riches that this good thing not turn to poison for his soul. Is he poor? — let him be poor in spirit as well, that he may receive the riches of God's goodness. Is he a soldier? — let him so make war as not to lose eternal life.

In a word: every Christian, in every calling and rank, must keep his first care and concern on this — not to be deprived of eternal salvation, for without it everything is nothing. And whoever holds this thought and this care, every calling and rank will help him towards salvation. Let every Christian's first care and concern, then, be for the salvation of his soul, as for the first and most necessary task, and by the grace of God he will be saved. For God almighty helps those who so strive and so labour.

sections.heading: Light from the Word of God

pairs.en: For this, enlightenment by the grace of God is needed; and enlightenment, with God's help, the Christian receives from the Holy Scripture. In Holy Scripture, God is set before us to be known, with His attributes and His holy will; there the old man and the new are described — the man who is perishing and the man who is being saved; there the way to salvation is shown, and the way to ruin. There you will see what meets every man after death — that is, in eternity.

Be assured, then, in very truth, that the Holy Scripture is the Word of God, and that it is spoken for you, as for every man. It was given you for the obtaining of eternal salvation: seek your salvation in it. Leave off inquiring into what is happening in this place or that; inquire rather, out of the Word of God, into what is happening in your own soul, and towards what end you are travelling — towards ruin, or towards salvation; on the way of the righteous, or on the way of the ungodly. Be assured beyond doubt that God appeared in the flesh for no other purpose than to save you, and all men, for eternal life.
O truly great deed, past the mind's grasp: God appeared in the flesh for the sake of man, His unprofitable servant! Blessed is God, whose good pleasure this was!

Keep in remembrance this great deed, than which there is no greater, and ponder it, and you will be enlightened. Be assured that God is in every place; that He sees your every deed, undertaking and thought, and hears your every word, and writes it in His book, and in the last day will declare it all to you, and render to you according to it all. *“I will rebuke thee, and set thy sins in order before thine eyes,”* says God Himself through the prophet. [Psalm 49:21] Fix this fast in your memory — and you will be made new every day.

Be assured, without any doubt, that in the holy Eucharist you truly partake of the Body and Blood of Christ. Be assured that there will be a resurrection of the dead in the last day, and every man will rise either to eternal life or to eternal condemnation. Be firmly assured that the universal judgment of Christ will come, and a strict examination of deeds, words and thoughts, and that the day will come unlooked-for; and write upon your heart that the day is already near. *Soon the Lord will come, and will not tarry,* and He will call all men before Him to judgment. Write this, I beg you, upon your heart, so that it never leave your memory. Be assured that there will be eternal torment for the ungodly, and eternal life for the righteous.

You see your brethren carried out of their houses and buried in the earth: remember that you too are *earth, and to earth you shall return*. [Genesis 3:19] They leave everything behind; so will you. At their death they came to the great judgment on all worldly things — that everything in this world is *vanity, and vanity of vanities* [Ecclesiastes 1:2]; so will you. At their death no one could help them — not household, nor friends, nor neighbours, nor glory, nor honour, nor riches; and no one will help you. All things abandoned them; all things will abandon you. They trembled then before the judgment of God, for that belongs to all men; you too will tremble. But blessed is he who *dies in the Lord* — for such a one the Lord does not abandon when everything else abandons him.

Therefore do not abandon the Lord now, so that He may not abandon you then. Please Him now, as a servant pleases his lord, so that then He may own you for His servant, and stretch out to you His almighty hand, and deliver your soul from your enemies the demons, who in that hour roar like lions and would devour us. Remember the hour of death, beloved: dreadful is that hour, not to sinners only, but to the saints themselves. All their life long they kept it in remembrance, and in contrition of heart prayed to Him who is able to save them.

Therefore turn from vanity to truth, from the world and from sin to God, from time to eternity; and casting aside all the world's amusements, come to the sacred Bible, and hold to the Word of God written in it, and it will enlighten you and guide you to eternal life — and hold to it without swerving.

See what is done in the world. Christians now, for the greater part, count the task of salvation not as the first task but as the last — or as nothing at all. For some it is no sin to break the law of God, holy and eternal: they count it no sin to commit fornication, to seize and to steal, to use violence, to do wrong, to draw the tears of widows and orphans, to lead others astray, to lie, to cheat, to abuse, to slander, to blaspheme, and to do whatever else is like these. Others study only how to win vain glory, honour and riches. Others spend their pains on building and adorning rich houses, dressing in rich and beautiful clothing, laying rich tables, driving out with rich carriages and horses, paying visits and receiving guests, and contriving one amusement after another. This is their first task; and on their first task they spend their first care. For what a man purposes in his heart, that he does, and for that he labours.

These people, as is plain, count the great task of eternal salvation — for the sake of which God Himself came into the world, lived upon the earth, laboured, suffered and died in the flesh — as a small thing, or almost as nothing; and so they hold in no honour the very One who came into the world and accomplished the work of salvation. For whoever cares little about a thing counts it a little thing; and whoever cares nothing at all about it counts it as nothing.

O salvation — eternal salvation, bought at so dear a price, the Blood and death of the Son of God — how cheap it is among the Christians of today! What is dear to them now is whatever pleases *the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life*. [1 John 2:16]

O man, who carry the name of Christ but do not follow the teaching of Christ! Do you neglect that for which our Christ laboured on earth thirty-three years and more, and drank the most bitter cup of suffering? If you do not see it now, you will see in eternity that everything you labour for is nothing — mere delusion, a device of Satan invented for man's destruction — and that eternal salvation is the most necessary task, the *one thing needful*, without which everything is nothing.

This is what it is to throw away the pearl of great price and grasp at refuse; to leave the truth and chase a shadow; and, in the apostle's word, *to receive the grace of God in vain*. [2 Corinthians 6:1] God sent His only-begotten Son into the world to save us, the perishing. This deed is so great that it passes the understanding not of men only but of angels. Yet Christians, who know of it, set it aside as a small thing; and despising this great grace of God, throwing away, as it were, the pearl of great price held out to them, they grasp at what is in itself nothing. Therefore the anger of God will burn hot against them, and it will be more bearable for the men of Sodom, for the pagans, the idolaters and the Turks in the day of judgment than for such Christians.

Do not imitate such Christians. *Fret not because of evildoers, neither be envious against the workers of iniquity: for they shall soon be withered like the grass, and fade as the green herb.* [Psalm 36:1–2] Do not imitate those who think only of earthly things; but strive to live by the rule of the Word of God, and be in this world *a stranger and a pilgrim* [1 Chronicles 29:15] — if you would have eternal salvation for your first task, and receive with thanksgiving this grace of God given to us — and so you will be saved.
I know that you will ask me: what does it mean, to be a stranger and a pilgrim in this world?

I answer. Whoever is far from his fatherland and his home, and finds himself in a foreign country, is a stranger there and a pilgrim — as a Russian in the German lands, or in the Turkish, lives there a stranger and a pilgrim. So the Christian — far from his heavenly fatherland and from the house of God, and living in this world of many troubles — is a stranger and a pilgrim.

A man journeying in a foreign land is wary of everything. So the Christian, living in this world, is wary of everything and guards himself: against the demons, against sin, against the world's seductions, against evil men; even parents, kinsfolk and old acquaintances — all who set their minds *on things on the earth, and not on things above* [Colossians 3:2] — he holds in suspicion.

A journeying man acquires nothing immovable in a foreign land, and builds nothing — no houses, no gardens, nothing beyond the needful, without which he could not live. So for the true Christian, everything in this world is what immovable property is to the traveller: honour, glory, riches, gold, silver, villages, houses, ponds, gardens, groves, land, carriages, horses, cattle, clothing and all the rest. As a man leaving a foreign country leaves behind everything that cannot be moved, so the Christian will leave everything in the world — and the body itself. Of this the holy apostle says: *“We brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out”*; and therefore, *“having food and raiment, let us be therewith content.”* [1 Timothy 6:7–8]

A journeying man sends his movable goods — his money and his wares — ahead of him into his fatherland, or carries them with him. For the true Christian, the movable goods of this world — the goods he can take with him and carry over into the age to come — are the virtues: love, mercy, patience, meekness, chastity and the rest. These he strives to gather here, while he lives in the world, as a spiritual merchant gathers spiritual wares, and to carry them over into that age, and to appear with them in his heavenly fatherland, and stand before his heavenly Father. To this Christ our Lord exhorts us: brethren, *“lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”* [Matthew 6:20–21]

Everyone shuns the journeying man and keeps his distance, as from one not their own, a foreigner. So all the lovers of this world, the sons of this age, shun the true Christian, and keep far from him, and persecute him, as one not their own and of no use to them. Of this Christ says: *“If ye were of the world, the world would love his own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you.”* [John 15:19] They say the sea casts up its dead upon the shore: so the world casts out the man who has died to the world. And every stranger and pilgrim in this world must be dead to the world.

For the journeying man, life in a foreign land is dreary. So for the true Christian it is dreary and sorrowful to live in this world: to him the world is everywhere an exile, a prison, a place of banishment, far as he is from his heavenly fatherland. Yet the journeying man, dreary as his life abroad may be, lives there nonetheless, for the sake of the need that took him from home. So the true Christian, though it is sorrowful for him to live in this world, lives on and endures it for as long as God commands.

The journeying man keeps his fatherland and his home always in mind and memory, and longs and hastens to return. The Jews in Babylon longed always to return to Jerusalem, their fatherland. So the true Christian sits in this world as by the rivers of Babylon, and weeps when he remembers Jerusalem on high, the heavenly fatherland, and sighs, and longs to come there. *“For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven,”* says holy Paul with all the faithful. [2 Corinthians 5:2]

This, then, is what it is to be a stranger and a pilgrim in this world. And that all Christians must be strangers and pilgrims in this world is plain too from the apostle's word, spoken of all Christians together: *“For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.”* [Hebrews 13:14]
Be a stranger, then, in this world, and hold heaven for your fatherland, and your first task will be the task of salvation — and so, by the grace of God, you will be saved.
Be saved.
